claims.text: Controlled electrochemical polarization of 316L stainless steel induces a passive surface film.
The polarization-induced passive film is continuous.
The polarization-induced passive film is rich in Cr2O3.
The polarization-induced passive film is self-healing.
The induced passive film significantly reduces the corrosion rate of 316L stainless steel under chemical-processing conditions.
Under oxidizing conditions, chromium in 316L stainless steel oxidizes to form Cr2O3.
The resulting Cr2O3 layer is dense.
The Cr2O3 layer resists ion penetration.
The passive film repairs minor surface damage.
Repair of minor damage maintains passive-film integrity and corrosion resistance.
Polarized samples will have lower corrosion current densities than untreated samples.
Polarized samples will have higher EIS impedance values than untreated samples.
Polarized samples will exhibit delayed passive-film breakdown during cyclic testing relative to untreated samples.
The proposed effect is expected to hold in synthetic process fluids containing 0–5 wt% chloride at 25–90 °C.
Applicability beyond the specified laboratory conditions is uncertain.
The long-term stability and evolution of the polarized passive film under dynamic service conditions are uncertain.
A laboratory-induced passive film may not fully reproduce passive-film formation during service.
Untreated 316L samples exposed under otherwise identical conditions constitute the experimental baseline.
The controlled study varies chloride concentration from 0 to 5 wt% and temperature from 25 to 90 °C while using cyclic potentiodynamic polarization and EIS.
The hypothesis is falsified if polarized samples show no statistically significant improvement in corrosion current density, impedance, or film-breakdown behavior relative to untreated samples.
